reading.title: Why Fair Clubs Need Clear Rules
reading.purpose: Consider an argument for building school activities that welcome every student fairly.
paras: Each fall, middle schools open dozens of clubs, from chess to robotics. Too often, students think a sign-up sheet alone makes a club fair. In truth, a club is fair only when its rules protect equity, giving each student the help needed for a real chance to join and grow. If a robotics club charges a high supply fee, that cost creates inequality between homes with extra cash and those without.

Fairness also rests on how leaders judge skill. Tryouts must stay impartial, treating each student evenly without favoring old friends. When judges let prejudice—an unfair view formed before checking the facts—guide their scores, strong new voices get pushed out. Using a lazy stereotype, like saying quiet kids cannot lead a debate, causes clubs to discriminate against students who speak in a calmer style.

Club leaders should judge work on real merit, rewarding skill, effort, and clear work rather than fame. When a school uses blind tryouts—such as hearing music players behind a screen—judges cannot easily exclude a student based on looks or past rumors. A good school should not tolerate unfair walls just because "that is how we did it last year."

Some people say that loaner gear, fee waivers, and clear score sheets take extra time. They are right—it does take work. Yet a school shows real integrity when it sticks to honest rules even when doing so takes extra care. Opening the door wide does not lower the bar. It makes sure every student's skill gets a fair shot.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "impartial" most nearly means
choices: choosing only students who have joined the club before
treating every applicant fairly without favoring one side
charging a higher fee to pay for extra robotics supplies
listening to speeches only from the loudest club members
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines impartial directly as "treating every applicant evenly without favoring old friends."

qs.q: Which sentence gives a concrete method schools use to judge auditions fairly?
choices: Club leaders should judge work on real merit, rewarding skill, effort, and clear work rather than fame.
When a school uses blind tryouts—such as hearing music players behind a screen—judges cannot easily exclude a student based on looks or past rumors.
A good school should not tolerate unfair walls just because "that is how we did it last year."
It makes sure every student's skill gets a fair shot.
qs.why: This sentence names a specific practice—hearing music players behind a screen—to keep judging focused on performance.

ev.text: When a school uses blind tryouts—such as hearing music players behind a screen—judges cannot easily exclude a student based on looks or past rumors.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the objection that fair systems take extra planning?
choices: By admitting the extra work is real, then arguing that sticking to honest principles is worth it.
By claiming that loaner gear and written rubrics require almost no time from teachers.
By suggesting that schools should cancel robotics and debate teams until fees drop.
By agreeing that old traditions should be kept whenever a club has limited money.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 concedes "it does take effort" and counters that real integrity means upholding fair principles even when it is harder.

qs.q: What is the author's main claim in this argument?
choices: Middle schools should stop holding auditions and let every student join every team automatically.
Sign-up sheets are the best way to prevent stereotypes from affecting after-school activities.
School clubs become truly fair only when clear rules remove money barriers and biased judging.
Quiet students perform much better in music auditions than they do in school debate clubs.
qs.why: The argument contends that fair clubs need equity, impartial rubrics, and blind auditions so merit—not barriers or bias—decides outcomes.

clues.text: giving each student the help needed for a real chance to join and grow
an unfair view formed before checking the facts
rewarding skill, effort, and clear work rather than fame
sticks to honest rules even when doing so takes extra care

reading.retellFrame: The author argues that school clubs are truly fair when they remove ___ and judge students by ___.
